title: No ranking
hookLine: the voices of this block keep company with pain; none of them asks anyone to rank it or compare it to someone else's

cards: "At least it's not cancer." "Other people have it so much worse." "I shouldn't complain, after what she's been through."
These lines get said with the best intentions, sometimes to a friend, often to ourselves. They sound humble. But listen to what they do.

They put pain on a scale, and somebody's pain has to lose. Across this whole block, from Job to Julian to Frankl, the texts keep company with suffering in many ways. They don't line it up and rank it.

teach.h: JOB'S FRIENDS SAT, AND SAID NOTHING.
teach.b: First, Job's friends, at their best.
When they arrive, the King James Bible says: "So they sat down with him upon the ground seven days and seven nights, and none spake a word unto him: for they saw that his grief was very great."
They didn't measure it against anyone's. They sat in it with him. It's when they start explaining and weighing that the book turns against them.
Second, Paul, to the church in Rome: "Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep." Weep with, not weigh against. Paul sets it in a list of ways to live alongside each other.
Third, Frankl, a man who had every reason to rank.

teach.h: LIKE A GAS, IT FILLS THE ROOM.
teach.b: In Man's Search for Meaning he offers a picture, in paraphrase: suffering behaves like a gas in an empty room. A little gas or a lot, it fills the whole room.
So a person's suffering, great or small, fills the whole of them. The size of suffering, he says, is relative, and comparing doesn't shrink anything.
Fourth, the week. Shu showed a gift the world's measure missed. Julian heard a promise said with no blame.

Ivan refused to let one child's tears be outweighed. Frankl found meaning inside the camps, and Helen found a word at the pump. Not one of them asked anyone to prove their pain was big enough to count.
Ranking doesn't make anyone's pain smaller. It just leaves someone alone with theirs.

how: In Jewish mourning, visitors to a shiva house may wait for the mourner to speak first, and Christians read Romans 12:15 as a call to share both joy and grief; some chaplains and counselors are taught not to compare one person's pain with another's.

o: treating every pain as exactly the same size
keeping company with pain without weighing it
saying others have it worse, to stay humble

games.q: inside no ranking — tap the pairs.
p: sat with him and said nothing

s: Job's friends went wrong the moment they arrived
at first they sat with him in silence; it went wrong when they started explaining.
Frankl compared suffering to a gas that fills a whole room
great or small, it fills the person completely.
Paul's line says to weigh another's grief against your own
it says weep with them that weep.

games.q: your friend tells you about a hard week. your own week was much worse. what do you say?
o: at least you didn't have my week.
that sounds hard. tell me about it.
games.why: Job's friends did best when they just sat with him, and Paul's line is weep with, not weigh against. their week fills them the way yours fills you.

practice: Let something that hurts right now come to mind, big or small, and notice if a voice shows up to compare it: at least, others have it worse, I shouldn't. When it does, set the scale down and let your own thing be the size it is.
Then, if you like, bring someone else who's hurting to mind, and let theirs be its size too: two pains side by side, neither one weighed.

wordCard.voice: No ranking. Pain kept company with, not weighed against anyone else's: weep with them that weep. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: weep with them that weep. The week held Shu, Julian, the question stays, meaning, Frankl, water, and no ranking. That's day seven hundred thirty-five, and a week.
